value.overview: The Rufous-tailed Hummingbird is a widespread, medium-sized hummingbird of tropical America. It is especially common around forest edges, gardens, plantations, clearings, and flowering shrubs. Its bright green plumage, reddish bill, and rich rufous tail make it distinctive. Active and assertive, it frequently defends concentrated nectar sources from other hummingbirds. The species adapts well to many human-modified landscapes but also uses natural woodland, scrub, gallery forest, and mangrove edges.
value.classification: Scientific name: Amazilia tzacatl. It belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the order Apodiformes.
value.identification: Adults are about 9–11 cm long and generally appear glittering green above, with green extending across much of the breast. The belly is grayish or buffy, while the tail and uppertail coverts are conspicuously rufous to chestnut. The bill is straight and medium-long, with a reddish lower mandible and dark tip; the upper mandible is mostly dark. Males and females are similar, although females may be slightly duller. The rufous tail is especially noticeable when spread in flight.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from eastern and southern Mexico through Central America, including Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama. Its South American range includes parts of Colombia, western Venezuela, and western Ecuador. It inhabits humid and semi-humid forest edges, secondary growth, thickets, gallery woodland, mangrove margins, plantations, gardens, and other semi-open areas. It generally favors lowlands and foothills but locally occurs at elevations approaching 2,500 meters.
value.migrationStatus: Primarily resident. Some populations make local or seasonal movements, including shifts in elevation that follow flowering plants.
value.breeding: Breeding dates vary geographically and may extend across much of the year in favorable tropical areas. The female builds a compact cup nest from plant fibers and down, binding it with spider silk and decorating the exterior with lichens or moss. It is usually placed on a horizontal branch or in a fork within a shrub or small tree. The typical clutch contains two white eggs. The female alone incubates them for about 15–16 days and feeds the chicks, which usually fledge after roughly 18–22 days.
value.dietFeeding: The Rufous-tailed Hummingbird feeds mainly on flower nectar, visiting many native and cultivated plants, including trees, shrubs, vines, and herbs. It hovers at blossoms and may also perch while feeding. Small insects and spiders provide protein and are gleaned from leaves and branches or captured in flight. Individuals regularly patrol productive flower patches and often drive other hummingbirds away with rapid chases and diving attacks.
value.behavior: This hummingbird is active, conspicuous, and strongly territorial around rich nectar sources. It frequently perches in exposed locations, watching for competitors before launching into swift pursuits. Its flight is direct and agile, with the hovering ability typical of hummingbirds. Birds are usually encountered alone rather than in cohesive flocks, although several may gather where flowers are abundant. Males do not form lasting pairs or assist with nesting; courtship and mating are their principal reproductive roles.

conservation.status: Least Concern on the IUCN Red List.
conservation.populationTrend: Decreasing globally, although the species remains widespread and locally common.
